content: 1. The implementation guide toolkit provides a structured approach to stakeholder mapping, specifically for identifying and engaging key stakeholders in the delivery of reproductive health and family planning services. This is done in preparation for integrating and implementing the World Health Organization (WHO) Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) and Selected Practice Recommendations (SPR) guidance into national programs. 2. Stakeholder mapping involves three key steps: learning about the process of stakeholder mapping, exploring and understanding the sample stakeholder mapping grid, and completing your own stakeholder mapping grid. 3. Potential stakeholders are individuals or organizations that have an interest in or the ability to influence the integration and implementation of WHO guidance into national family planning programs. This includes their leadership and organizational roles. 4. Stakeholder perspectives should be used to inform a country’s strategy for implementing and integrating the MEC and SPR into national family planning guidelines. This ensures that the process is inclusive and considers diverse viewpoints. 5. At the beginning of the implementation process, the core implementation team must define the roles of stakeholders to facilitate effective engagement. This step is critical for ensuring the success of the initiative. 6. Stakeholder mapping is a method used by the implementation team to understand the perspectives, affiliations, and areas of representation of stakeholders. It also identifies their interests and contributions to the integration of MEC and SPR into national family planning guidelines. 7. To use this tool effectively, it is important to first understand what a stakeholder is and what stakeholder mapping entails. Stakeholder mapping is the process of analyzing and prioritizing stakeholders based on their influence, interests, and roles in the implementation process. 8. To identify key stakeholders in reproductive health and family planning service delivery, consider everyone who may have an interest in the implementation team’s objectives, both currently and in the future. This list of stakeholders may evolve over time. 9. It is not always practical or necessary to engage with all stakeholder groups with the same level of intensity throughout the process. The level and phase of engagement should be tailored to the specific needs of the implementation process. 10. Mapping relationships between objectives and stakeholder roles involves analyzing how each stakeholder can contribute to the successful incorporation of updated MEC and SPR recommendations into national policies. 11. To analyze stakeholder perspectives, interests, roles, and engagement in the implementation process, consider the following: What is the mission of their organization, and what is their primary contribution to reproductive health and family planning? What is the desired outcome of their efforts? What motivates their work? What is their capacity to engage in the implementation process? Are they supportive or critical of the family planning guidance or the proposed implementation process? 12. Whenever possible, engage directly with stakeholders to understand their interests and potential roles in the planning and implementation of WHO MEC and SPR guidance. 13. Prioritizing stakeholder engagement should be informed by the analysis of their influence and interests. Stakeholders with a high level of influence should be prioritized for engagement at the outset of the implementation process. 14. All stakeholders contribute to the implementation of family planning guidance, but it is important to consider the appropriate level and phase of engagement for each stakeholder. 15. The sample stakeholder mapping grid, adapted from Business for Social Responsibility (BSR) and the International Association of Public Participation (IAP2), provides a practical framework for organizing and analyzing stakeholder relationships and roles in the implementation process.
